Syllabus

CSS 555 · Evaluating Software Design · Winter 2027draft

Vitals

  • Course Number and Title: CSS 555: Evaluating Software Design
  • Description: "Studies best software engineering practices and methods used in prescriptive and agile approached to create and evaluate software design from an quality principled point-of-view. Considers design from quality dimensions such as performance, scalability, maintainability, usability, and security." (University of Washington Bothell, CSS course catalog, 2026–27)
  • Meeting Time/Place: TBD (planned as Monday/Wednesday, 2-hour sessions).
  • Credit: 5 units. This translates into 10–11 hours of work per week outside of class.
  • Notice: Contents of this Syllabus and the course web site can change at any time in the term.
  • Class Culture:
    • Excellence: I have high standards. You are expected to meet them.
    • Initiative: Ask questions! Engage and wrestle with the material, your colleagues, and myself.
    • Grace: Freedom to learn and grow. Extend courtesy to each other.

Topics and Learning Objectives

Topics: evaluation as evidence and quality models; measurement theory and empirical method (scales, Goal-Question-Metric, validity); measurable quality requirements (scenarios, SLIs, SLOs); architecture reviews (ATAM, ARID, TARA, lightweight reviews); performance, scalability, and resilience; maintainability at module and architecture level, from structure and from change and defect history; usability; security; continuous evaluation with fitness functions and conformance checks; tradeoff analysis and reporting findings.

Learning Objectives: By the end of this course, students will:

  1. Specify quality goals as measurable quality-attribute scenarios and service-level objectives.
  2. Conduct a scenario-based architecture evaluation (ATAM or ARID) and report risks, non-risks, sensitivity points, and tradeoff points.
  3. Predict performance and scalability analytically (Little's Law, the Universal Scalability Law) and validate the prediction with load tests.
  4. Assess maintainability at module and architecture level, from structure (coupling, cohesion, dependency structure, design smells) and from change and defect history (hotspots, architectural debt).
  5. Evaluate usability with inspection methods and a small user study.
  6. Threat-model a design (STRIDE, attack trees) and verify it against OWASP ASVS.
  7. Encode quality expectations and architecture rules as automated fitness functions in a CI pipeline.
  8. Design measurements that can support a claim (scales, Goal-Question-Metric, repetition) and critique evaluation evidence for validity threats and metric gaming.

Course Structure

The spine of the course is predict, then measure. Each catalog dimension gets two evaluations:

  • Analytical (prescriptive): reason about the design before running it, using models, structure, and reviews.
  • Empirical (agile): measure the running system or mine its history.

You write the prediction down before measuring, then explain the gap. The gap is where the learning is.

Scope. The course evaluates design at every level: the architecture, the modules and their interfaces, and the structure of the code. The implementation is the main source of evidence: the running system, the code, and its history. Functional correctness is not a course topic; finding bugs belongs to testing. Defect data counts only as evidence about the design: where bug fixes cluster says something about the modules they touch.

Part Weeks Theme Core Question
I 1–2 What Counts as Evidence What would convince us a design is good?
II 3–5 Performance, Scalability, Resilience Will it be fast enough, grow, and survive failure?
III 5–7 Maintainability and Usability Can people change it, and can people use it?
IV 8–9 Security and Continuous Evaluation Can it be attacked, and how do we keep checking?
V 10 Synthesis What should the decision makers do?

Session format (with some variation): paper critique (~15 min, Sessions 3–16), lecture (~60 min), ICA or lab (~45 min).

Where this course sits. CSS 553 (Software Architecture, Spring) teaches how to design for a quality; this course teaches how to tell whether a design achieved it; CSS 478 (Usability and User-Centered Design, Spring) works with the people who use the system. Neither CSS 553 nor CSS 478 is a prerequisite: Sessions 2 and 3 introduce scenarios and ATAM from the start.

See the schedule for dates, readings, and due dates.

Requirements

Pre-Class Activities (PCA): Readings listed in the schedule are due before the session they are listed under. Sessions with assigned reading have a short Canvas reading quiz, due at the start of class.

In-Class Activities (ICA): Structured team exercises (scenario writing, mini-reviews, threat modeling, a usability pilot). Submitted on Canvas by the end of class; graded on completion and good-faith effort.

Labs: Five labs on a shared reference app (TeaStore): load testing, scalability fitting, fault injection, history mining, and security scanning. Each lab report states the prediction, the method, the data, and the gap. Due before the next session.

Evaluation Project: See Evaluation Project.

Paper Critique: Each student gives one 8-minute individual critique of a paper from the schedule's paper list: the claim, the evidence, what the evidence does not show, and what it means for evaluating designs today. Slides carry figures, charts, and diagrams only, no bullet text. Sign up by Week 1 Wednesday.

Midterm: None. Milestones E1 and E2 assess the first half of the course.

Final Exam: In class, individual, 120 minutes, cumulative. You evaluate an unseen design document with accompanying measurement data: write scenarios, identify risks and tradeoffs, and judge which claims the data support. Closed book; one double-sided handwritten reference sheet.

Evaluation Project

Teams of 3–4 evaluate one open-source system across the quarter and deliver an evaluation a real team could act on.

System requirements (instructor approval at E0):

  • Runs locally with Docker Compose
  • Has a user interface and a documented API
  • At least 10K lines of code and 2 years of public git history

House system (pre-approved). The UWB social network built by CSS 553 in Spring 2026: 19 services on a Docker Swarm platform with monitoring, OpenAPI contracts, and ADRs, deployable on one host. It is exempt from the history requirement. With the team's written permission, a house-system E4 report becomes the inherited evaluation that CSS 553 teams start from in Spring 2027. Its git authors are pseudonymized; do not try to identify them.

Milestones:

Milestone Deliverable Due Points
E0 Evaluation plan: system choice, utility tree with 10–15 measurable scenarios across all five dimensions, method and measurement plan (Goal-Question-Metric) per scenario Sun Jan 17 15
E1 Performance, scalability, resilience: predictions, load and fault tests, USL fit, gap analysis Sun Feb 7 45
E2 Maintainability: module- and architecture-level structural metrics, design smells, hotspot, defect, and architectural-debt analysis Sun Feb 21 35
E3 Usability and security: heuristic evaluation, 5-user test with SUS, threat model, ASVS Level 1 check Sun Mar 7 45
E4 Final report in ATAM form (risks, non-risks, sensitivity and tradeoff points, risk themes), fitness functions and conformance checks in CI, presentation Presentations Mar 8 and 10; report Sun Mar 14 60
Total 200

Milestones are due at 11:59 PM PT. Every finding states its prediction, method, data, and the main threat to its validity. Each milestone includes a short statement of who contributed what.

Testing rules:

  • Load tests, fault injection, and security scans target only the reference app and your own local deployment of the project system. Never point them at a public instance or any system you do not own or have written permission to test.
  • Usability tests are a classroom exercise, not research. Participants are classmates or volunteers, participation is voluntary, and no identifying data leaves the team's notes.

Make-Up and Late Policy

Deliverables are due at the stated date and time. Late work loses 10% per day; the maximum grade for any late submission is 90%.

Lowest score drops:

  • Pre-Class Activities: 2 reading quizzes
  • In-Class Activities: 2 ICAs
  • Labs: 0

The drops cover a missed session or a bad week without paperwork. Labs are not dropped because each one feeds a project milestone.

Exceptions: Extensions are granted for documented health issues, bereavement, university business, and legal obligations.

Request an extension before the deadline whenever possible; requests made after the fact require documentation of why advance notice was impossible.

Extra Credit

None.

AI Policy

AI tools are permitted and expected for tooling: load-test scripts, analysis notebooks, plots, scanner configuration. Evaluation claims are yours. A finding must rest on your own measurements and reasoning; a claim with no data behind it counts as unsupported, whoever wrote it.

  • Disclosure: each milestone lists the AI tools used, what for, and where they were wrong.
  • Session 15 makes this explicit: an LLM reviews your system's design, and you grade its review against your own evidence.
  • Safety: commit before letting an agent change files; verify that AI-suggested dependencies exist; never commit secrets.

Collaboration & Academic Integrity

Evaluation is a team sport; collaboration within your project team is expected, and discussing methods with other teams is encouraged.

Guidelines:

  • For labs and the project: Teams share work freely internally. Do not share data, scripts, or write-ups between teams. Cite any public dataset, benchmark, or prior evaluation you build on.
  • For writing assignments: Write your own analysis. Quoted or paraphrased material must be cited. AI-generated text follows the AI Policy: disclosed, checked, and backed by your data.
  • For quizzes and exams: Individual work only.

Internet and programming resources:

  • Small snippets: attribute if non-obvious
  • Substantial blocks: must cite source and mark copied lines
  • Ideas from other code: attribute non-obvious ideas
  • Copyrighted code: note in comments; do not distribute without permission

Due process: Suspected violations are referred under the UW Student Conduct Code, which describes your rights and the appeal process.
